A1-A2.headline: Why the UK Stopped Killing Badgers

pages.text: Badgers are wild animals. For years, the UK let people kill some badgers to try to stop a disease in cows. This is called culling. By May 2026, this practice had ended. The government wanted to use vaccines instead. Vaccines help protect animals from disease.
pages.caption: A European badger in its natural home.

pages.text: The UK has a law to protect badgers. The law dates from 1992. It says that people must not hurt badgers or damage their homes without legal permission. Badgers live in holes in the ground. The law helps keep these wild animals and their homes safe.
pages.caption: The entrance to a badger home.

evidence.articleCaption: The entrance to a badger sett down which gas canisters are thrown during gassing

pages.text: Scientists studied what happened when people killed badgers. Some badgers that were left moved to other places. This could help the disease spread to new areas. The results were not simple. It was hard to know how well killing badgers would help stop the disease.

By 2024, the country had spent more than 58 million pounds on killing badgers. Now the government wants to use vaccines to help fight the disease. The aim is to keep farm animals healthy and help farmers. It is not yet clear how well the new plan will work.

B1-B2.headline: Changing Strategies for Bovine Tuberculosis in the UK

pages.text: For years, the United Kingdom used badger control to manage bovine tuberculosis in cattle. This disease, caused by bacteria, was a major challenge for farmers. However, the policy has ended. As of May 2026, no active licences remain, marking a shift toward vaccination. Experts note that while this change is significant, the long-term impact on disease rates remains uncertain.
pages.caption: A European badger in the wild.

pages.text: Despite their role in disease, European badgers are protected wild animals. The Protection of Badgers Act 1992 keeps them safe from harm. This legal status made the control policy controversial, as it required special licences to bypass these rules. Many groups argued that the animals deserved better protection, especially given the lack of clear evidence regarding the safety and success of the policy.
pages.caption: The entrance to a badger sett.

evidence.articleCaption: The entrance to a badger sett down which gas canisters are thrown during gassing

pages.text: Scientific trials showed mixed results. Researchers found a movement effect, where the loss of badgers caused survivors to travel further. This change in their social structure actually helped spread the disease to new areas. Because of this, many experts questioned if the programme was effective, noting that the results were not as positive as some had hoped for in the beginning.

The cost of the policy was high, reaching 58.8 million pounds by 2024. With the end of the programme, the government is now using vaccination to manage the disease. This approach aims to support animal welfare while reducing the economic burden on farmers. Officials remain cautious, however, as the effectiveness of these new methods is still being monitored for future safety.

C1-C2.headline: The Evolution of UK Bovine Tuberculosis Control Policies

pages.text: The United Kingdom has long grappled with the management of bovine tuberculosis, a persistent threat to cattle populations. Historically, badger culling was implemented as a primary control measure to mitigate the spread of Mycobacterium bovis. Following years of intense debate, the practice has been phased out, with all culling licences effectively expiring by May 2026.
pages.caption: A European badger in its habitat.

pages.text: Badgers occupy a unique position in British wildlife law, protected by the stringent Protection of Badgers Act 1992. This legislation reflects a societal commitment to animal welfare that often clashed with agricultural interests. The legal framework surrounding these animals necessitated a delicate balance between disease control and the preservation of a protected species.
pages.caption: A badger sett entrance.

evidence.articleCaption: The entrance to a badger sett down which gas canisters are thrown during gassing

pages.text: Scientific scrutiny of the culling trials highlighted the 'perturbation effect,' a phenomenon where the disruption of badger social structures inadvertently exacerbated disease transmission. By forcing survivors to migrate, the culling policy often facilitated the wider dispersal of the pathogen. These findings fundamentally undermined the rationale for continuing the cull as a viable disease management strategy.

The economic implications of the culling programme were profound, with costs exceeding 58.8 million pounds by 2024. The transition toward vaccination represents a strategic pivot, aiming to mitigate the disease's impact through more sustainable methods. This shift reflects a broader commitment to reconciling animal welfare standards with the economic realities of the agricultural sector.
